harness_change.description: tools/transciphering/bench/main.go: added a MachineState struct (readMachineState()) capturing cpu_governor, power_source (AC/battery, from /sys/class/power_supply/*/online and */status), load_avg_{1,5,15} (/proc/loadavg), cpu_count, and scaling_cur_mhz_{min,max} across all cores (/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq), captured immediately before the timed online-encrypt loop and embedded in every BenchResult JSON going forward. Prior bench output (results/*_r_fixed2.json and earlier) has no machine_state field -- this is a real gap this change closes, not retroactively fixed for old files.

machine_state_this_sweep.description: Stable across all 8 runs in this sweep (see per-result machine_state below for exact per-run values) -- governor, power source, and load average did not change mid-sweep; only scaling_cur_freq (an instantaneous powersave-governor sample) varied run to run, which is expected dynamic clocking behavior, not a confound.
machine_state_this_sweep.note: User was asked and chose to wait for AC power before this sweep ran, specifically because a prior session on this host found battery power caused 650-960 MHz clock clamping vs a 4.9 GHz ceiling. ADP0/online=1 confirmed immediately before running.

headline: NOT a clean repeat of 2026-08-18's ~0.48-0.82x. This same-session sweep gives a ratio that swings from 1.64x (Rubato MORE expensive, lane=1) to 0.64x (Rubato cheaper, lane=4) to 1.11x to 0.82x -- non-monotonic and crossing 1.0. This is reported as measured, not smoothed or re-run to get a 'cleaner' number. See comparison_to_2026-08-18 below for why this does not overturn the house rule that same-session ratios are more defensible than absolute latencies -- it does mean single-lane-count ratios at these small n (sub-millisecond per-call times) carry more noise than previously stated, and multi-lane trends should be read as a band, not a point estimate.

comparison_to_2026-08-18.description: artifacts/hera_vs_rubato_transciphering.json's axis_b (2026-08-18, powersave, AC, load 2.16/2.45/2.00, n=200) reported ratio_rubato_over_hera_mean of 0.484/0.723/0.819/0.701 at lanes 1/4/8/16 -- Rubato cheaper at every lane count. This sweep (2026-08-19, powersave, AC, load ~1.9-2.0, n=200, otherwise identical methodology and code) gives 1.640/0.643/1.112/0.824 -- Rubato MORE expensive at lanes 1 and 8, cheaper at 4 and 16. Both artifacts are kept; neither supersedes the other. Candidate cause: at n=200 rounds and sub-millisecond per-call cost (mean 0.08-1.6 ms across both ciphers and lane counts), scheduling jitter, GC pauses, and cache-state noise are a larger fraction of the measured time than the algebraic cost difference between the two ciphers -- consistent with the per-keystream-element micro-benchmark (cipher/block_bench_test.go, ns-resolution, -benchtime=100000x, -count=7) showing a much more stable ~0.57-0.77x Rubato/HERA ratio (see docs/MEASUREMENT_PROVENANCE.md rows 5-7), because that harness isolates the algebra from AEAD/quantization/per-call overhead and runs far more iterations. NOT independently re-verified by re-running the micro-benchmark this pass -- flagged as the more trustworthy per-element number on prior evidence, not re-confirmed today.
comparison_to_2026-08-18.implication: The per-record, per-lane-count ratio is measurably less stable across same-session-but-different-day runs than this repo previously stated. Do not cite a single by_lane_count ratio from either artifact as THE HERA-vs-Rubato per-record ratio; cite a range, or cite the per-keystream-element micro-benchmark ratio instead, which has much higher statistical power (700,000 iterations vs. 200) and is the more defensible number for a paper.
